focus.title: Mobile apps, under the hood
focus.body: I dig through Android APKs, DEX, JNI, and native code with traces, emulation, and traffic captures. A few matching signals don't mean two environments behave the same — I line up device, tool, and backend evidence before calling it.

focus.title: Backends with real boundaries
focus.body: APIs, WebSockets, and access checks are my kind of plumbing. Auth needs to happen before data goes out or limited resources get claimed. I test the 'nope' paths too, not just the happy path.

focus.title: Workers that don't leave a mess
focus.body: Queues, concurrent jobs, shutdowns, and unfinished work: the bits that get messy when a worker quits. I focus on who owns each task, what actually failed, and how to roll out changes without chaos.

focus.title: Infra without the guesswork
focus.body: Linux, containers, OpenWrt, and network rabbit holes. I check the config that's really active, then compare logs, metrics, and control requests. Routing, TLS, the app, and an external service are different suspects.

cases.title: Android integrity: under the hood
cases.summary: Real devices on one side, emulation on the other. I trace the native code, line up the inputs, and check where the two stories stop matching.
cases.context: I dig into how Android apps, native components, and backend verification fit together in integrity and attestation flows. The tricky bit is making sure the evidence belongs to the same run before blaming the device or the emulator.
cases.approach: Match the app build, version, profile, and inputs first. Then follow Java-to-JNI-to-native transitions, inspect traces and traffic, and check what makes it through the worker and backend contracts.
cases.focus: Repeatable runs, isolated diagnostics, and no mixing up 'the client produced output' with 'the intended server verifier accepted it.'
cases.disclosureNote: Private lab work. Sensitive artifacts stay private: no Play Integrity bypass claim, no accepted official verdict, and no claim that emulation fully matches a real device.

cases.title: WebSockets: auth before anything else
cases.summary: A realtime channel needs more than 'the socket connected.' I worked on auth, client/server coordination, failure paths, and keeping connection slots out of the wrong hands.
cases.context: Locking down HTTP routes doesn't magically lock down a realtime connection. The socket still needs to belong to the right session, and rejected connections need a clean way out.
cases.approach: Get the client and server speaking the same protocol. Authenticate before registering the socket, keep sensitive values out of URLs, and test missing or bad credentials as well as reconnects.
cases.focus: Check the access boundary on its own. A failed login check shouldn't turn into endless retries or eat somebody else's connection capacity.
cases.disclosureNote: An anonymized look at private engineering work. No service addresses, identifiers, specific findings, or claim about how the live system is doing right now.

cases.title: Workers that know when to quit
cases.summary: A worker shouldn't drop a mess on its way out. This work covers graceful shutdown, a bounded drain, and handing back only the unfinished tasks that worker owns.
cases.context: Workers stop. Updates happen. The trouble starts when a worker keeps grabbing jobs or loses track of task ownership during shutdown. That's how work gets stuck or handled twice.
cases.approach: Stop intake, give active work a deadline, then conditionally update only tasks owned by that worker instance. Repeated signals and transport failures get their own checks.
cases.focus: A shutdown you can observe and test, plus checks that the running instances match the source. A green build on its own doesn't cut it.
cases.disclosureNote: The engineering story, not the fleet's inside scoop. No infrastructure size, traffic numbers, private config, or current deployment claim.

cases.title: Mobile SDKs: same request, different story
cases.summary: Same-looking requests, different outcomes. I dig into SDK versions, app builds, launch state, and traffic to work out what changed under the hood.
cases.context: Swap an SDK, app build, platform, or install context and a familiar request can behave differently. A version number in the docs isn't enough — the specific build gets a look.
cases.approach: Inspect app packages and integration code, compare traffic and version behavior, and track where the inputs came from. Keep 'the code suggests this' separate from 'we watched it happen.'
cases.focus: One build doesn't speak for every build. Similar protocol structure isn't proof that the whole flow works with an external service.
cases.disclosureNote: Lab work on systems I own or have explicit permission to test. Private traces and requests stay private. Access to third-party systems isn't on offer.

cases.title: Push pipelines: queued isn't delivered
cases.summary: API → queue → worker → push provider. I check the handoffs, result access, transport failures, and task state — without calling 'queued' a delivery receipt.
cases.context: Taking a job doesn't mean the job ran, and running it doesn't mean the push arrived. Status and result endpoints need access checks too; they aren't a free pass around the original request.
cases.approach: Follow the API and background paths. Check who owns the result, what gets cached, and how transport failures show up. Internal task state and a provider's evidence are different things.
cases.focus: Keep results in the right hands and read statuses for what they actually mean. No delivery promises the provider hasn't backed up.

cases.title: Network debugging: one layer at a time
cases.summary: Routing, DNS, TLS, HTTP, then the app. I check each layer instead of letting one green health check call the whole thing healthy.
cases.context: A broken page doesn't automatically mean a broken route. And a happy health check doesn't prove the user's actual workflow works. Different signals, different questions.
cases.approach: Read the config that's active, run control requests, and compare logs and metrics against the competing theories. Keep experiments reversible; don't break the healthy bits just to test a hunch.
cases.focus: Find the cause, keep a control case, and separate 'we can reach it' from 'it responds' from 'the app actually works.'
cases.disclosureNote: Internal routes, addresses, and access details stay private. This is a portfolio, not a proxy or VPN service.

cases.title: Fenrir: a safer Tetris port
cases.summary: I built a firmware-specific CMF Phone 1 profile and added fail-closed checks to Fenrir's patching path. Exact image, exact partition, exact patch site — no 'close enough.'
cases.context: A broad pattern match is a rough place to put your trust when firmware changes between OTA builds. I dug into Fenrir on CMF Phone 1/Tetris and built a separate firmware-specific profile instead of quietly changing the generic Tetris path. The original Fenrir project is by R0rt1z2; this case is about my port and patch-safety work.
cases.approach: I added Tetris240910 for the 240910 firmware, tied it to an exact input SHA-256, and constrained patches by partition, expected match count, selected offset, and equal replacement length. I also wired those guard options through JSON-configured patch stages. A mismatch should stop the run, not pick a nearby match and hope for the best.
cases.focus: Make firmware drift loud and keep a port tied to the image it was built for. Alongside the port, I compared 24 Tetris firmware builds to track changes in preloader policy. That's static firmware analysis, not a compatibility stamp for every nearby version. The public PR documents the profile and device checks; this page doesn't turn screenshots or boot properties into an independently verified server-side verdict.
cases.disclosureNote: My contribution is PR #29 against R0rt1z2's Fenrir. At review time it was closed without merge, so I'm not presenting it as accepted upstream. The fork and PR are public; raw device artifacts stay private. This is a firmware-specific research contribution, not a universal port or an independently verified official attestation claim.

steps.title: Know what is running
steps.body: Start with the real build, config, inputs, and environment. The docs are a map, not proof that you're on the right road.

steps.title: Make the hunch testable
steps.body: Say what would prove the theory wrong. Get a repro before you reach for a fix.

steps.title: One change, one question
steps.body: Keep experiments small. Change five things at once and good luck figuring out which one mattered.

steps.title: Check the right thing
steps.body: A unit test, a device run, and a server response answer different questions. Don't swap one for another.

steps.title: Keep private stuff private
steps.body: Share the method and the takeaway, not private data. My own systems or explicit permission — that's the deal.
